summary: Describes a QoS NSLP quality-of-service model based on ITU-T Recommendation Y.1541 network QoS classes, with extra QSPEC parameters and processing guidelines. It is an Experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: A menu of ready-made service levels from the telecom standards body for reserving network quality.

subtitle: Quality-of-service framework based on ITU-T telecom standards for IP networks.

tldr.problem: Network operators need a way to define service levels for different applications across IP networks, from real-time voice to file transfers. Different applications have different tolerance for delay, jitter and packet loss, but there was no standard way to express these requirements for signaling across networks.
tldr.mechanism: The ITU-T Recommendation Y.1541 defines eight standardized QoS classes with specific performance objectives. This RFC extends NSIS QoS signaling to support Y.1541 classes by adding QSPEC parameters for traffic shape description and restoration priority, allowing Edge nodes to negotiate and reserve resources according to these predefined classes.
tldr.outcome: Networks can signal and reserve resources based on standardized service level agreements. Applications and service providers can work with a common set of QoS classes that map to real performance targets like 100 ms delay or 10^-3 packet loss, enabling consistent service delivery across domains.

today: RFC 5976 is Experimental. It provides a standardized way for networks to signal QoS using the ITU-T Y.1541 framework, but adoption has been limited. The specification remains on the Experimental path and has not progressed to Standards Track.

sections.title: QoS Classes Defined by Y.1541
sections.content:
Y.1541 is an ITU-T (International Telecommunication Union) recommendation that specifies eight QoS classes for IP networks. Each class defines performance objectives for one-way delay, delay variation (jitter), and packet loss ratio. This RFC implements a QoS model (Y.1541-QOSM) that brings these standardized classes into the NSIS QoS signaling framework.

The eight classes range from Class 0 (real-time, highly interactive, like video conferencing) to Class 5 (best-effort, like traditional internet traffic) to Classes 6 and 7 (loss-sensitive, like television transport or circuit emulation). By using Y.1541 classes, networks can offer predictable service levels based on internationally agreed-upon standards.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of Y.1541 as a global menu of service levels. Instead of each network inventing its own service names, they all use the same eight class names with the same performance targets. A class 0 service always means short delay and low loss, no matter which network offers it.

sections.title: Class Descriptions and Application Examples
sections.content:
Classes 0 and 1 are for real-time, interactive applications sensitive to jitter. Class 0 targets mean delay of 100 ms with 50 ms jitter and 10^-3 (one in 1000) loss. Class 1 allows up to 400 ms delay. Both support VoIP and video conferences. These classes typically map to Diffserv Expedited Forwarding (EF) behavior.

Classes 2, 3, and 4 support interactive transactions with no jitter requirement. Class 2 targets 100 ms delay, Class 3 allows 400 ms, Class 4 allows 1 second. All require low loss. These typically map to Diffserv Assured Forwarding (AF) classes. Class 5 is unspecified with no commitments, like traditional IP best-effort service. Classes 6 and 7 are extremely loss-sensitive (10^-5 loss ratio) for television transport, TDM circuit emulation, and high-capacity TCP. Class 6 targets 100 ms delay, Class 7 allows 400 ms.
sections.plainLanguage: Classes 0-1 are 'VoIP quality.' Classes 2-4 are 'reliable but slower.' Class 5 is 'whatever we have.' Classes 6-7 are 'super reliable for TV.' Each class has specific delay and loss targets that all networks understand the same way.

sections.title: Additional QSPEC Parameters for Y.1541
sections.content:
The RFC adds two new QSPEC parameters to the generic framework defined in RFC 5975. The Traffic Model (TMOD) Extension parameter adds a Peak Bucket Size (Bp) field, represented as a 32-bit IEEE floating-point number in octets. This parameter allows networks to specify the maximum burst size for traffic policing, improving traffic shaping accuracy for reservation-based admission control.

The Restoration Priority parameter adds information about how quickly and completely a flow should be restored if a network failure occurs. It contains three fields: Restoration Priority (3 levels: best-effort, normal, high), Time-to-Restore (desired recovery speed: unspecified, under 200 ms, or under 2 seconds), and Extent of Restoration (percentage of traffic restored: 100%, 80%, 60%). These fields allow service providers and customers to negotiate backup and recovery capabilities as part of the QoS agreement.
sections.plainLanguage: The Peak Bucket Size says how much data can be sent at once in a burst. The Restoration Priority says 'if something breaks, how fast do you need to fix it and how much of my traffic can you save?' This information helps networks plan their backup capacity.

sections.title: How Y.1541-QOSM Signaling Works
sections.content:
When a QoS NSIS initiator (QNI, typically an application or gateway) requests resources, it specifies a Y.1541 QoS Class number along with traffic parameters. At each network node along the path, the resource management function interprets the class and parameters to make admission control decisions.

The Y.1541-QOSM allows networks to accumulate performance metrics (delay, jitter, loss) across domains. When a class specifies a parameter (e.g., Class 0 specifies jitter, but Class 2 does not), nodes track that parameter across the path. If a lower class than desired can be achieved, nodes can report the available performance to help the QNI decide whether to accept the degraded service.

The signaling scheme combines per-flow requests at domain edges with aggregate handling in the interior, following standard Diffserv principles. Edge nodes translate Y.1541 class numbers and parameters into DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point) markings that interior routers understand.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask for class 0 quality. The first network says 'I can give you class 0.' The second network says 'My link is slow, but I can do class 1. Want that instead?' You get to decide based on what each network can deliver.

sections.title: Security Implications of Restoration Priority
sections.content:
The restoration priority parameter raises a potential security concern: a user could claim an emergency priority for their flows without legitimate need, effectively preventing real emergency calls from getting through. The RFC identifies this as a theft-of-service risk.

The RFC recommends several countermeasures. One approach is to restrict the emergency priority bit to authorized users (e.g., police). Another is to allow any user to set emergency priority only for certain destination addresses (e.g., fire departments, police). The specific policy depends on deployment scenarios and service provider agreements. Beyond restoration priority, the RFC relies on the security mechanisms of underlying protocols (RFC 5974 and RFC 5975).
sections.plainLanguage: If anyone can say 'my traffic is super important, restore it first,' they could block real emergencies. So only certain people should be allowed to use high priority, or it only works for specific destinations everyone agrees on.
